query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing Ta with Nb in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy (to form HfMoNbTiZr) will reduce the alloy density significantly while maintaining its excellent mechanical strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures (~1000 °C).
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy (density ~10.21 g/cm³, high strength at room and elevated temperatures)
generation.intervention: Substitute tantalum (Ta) completely with niobium (Nb) to obtain the revised composition HfMoNbTiZr.
generation.conditions: Mechanical performance will be evaluated at ambient (room) temperature and under high-temperature conditions up to approximately 1000 °C, using standard tensile or compression tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Maintaining the single-phase BCC (or disordered solid solution) microstructure, where the lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening are preserved despite the atomic substitution.
generation.mechanism: Ta contributes significantly to the alloy's high density (density ~16.65 g/cm³) compared to Nb (density ~8.57 g/cm³). By fully replacing Ta with Nb, the resulting weighted average density is reduced. Nb, being equally refractory, is expected to preserve the high-temperature stability and solid solution strengthening that provide the alloy’s excellent mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction in overall density potentially by 10-15% (target density approaching 8.6–9.0 g/cm³) while retaining mechanical strength at room temperature and near 1000 °C within approximately 10-15% of the original alloy’s performance.
generation.baseline: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of ~10.21 g/cm³ and demonstrated high strength at both room temperature and ~1000 °C.
generation.boundary: The performance is expected to be maintained under static load-bearing conditions from room temperature to ~1000 °C. A significant phase change or a degradation in mechanical properties beyond a 15% reduction in strength compared to the as-cast alloy would be beyond the acceptable boundaries.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding potential alterations in phase stability or microstructural evolution due to differences in atomic size and bonding between Ta and Nb. Any unforeseen phase instability or secondary phase precipitations at elevated temperatures could impact the predicted mechanical performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate the HfMoNbTiZr alloy using an as-cast route identical to that for HfMoTaTiZr. Perform density measurements, microstructural analyses (e.g., XRD, SEM) to confirm the presence of a single-phase BCC solid solution, and conduct mechanical tests (tensile and/or compressive) at room temperature and at ~1000 °C.
measurements: Phase identification and microstructure quality (via XRD and SEM)
Mechanical strength (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength) at room temperature and at ~1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-substituted HfMoNbTiZr exhibits a reduction in mechanical strength greater than 15% compared to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr or shows evidence of phase instability (e.g., formation of secondary phases), or if the density reduction is not observed as predicted, then the hypothesis is falsified.

These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. frame.system: The as‐cast equiatomic high‐entropy alloy HfMoTaTiZr, which is known for its high strength at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (~1000 °C) but suffers from a high density of about 10.21 g/cm³.
frame.goal: Reduce the alloy's density without sacrificing its mechanical strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures (~1000 °C).
frame.limitation: The alloy’s high density, which is not ideal for weight‐sensitive applications despite its attractive strength properties.
root_cause_cues: without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C
constraints: The intervention must be a single change in alloy composition (a single intervention).
Mechanical properties must remain robust at both room temperature and around 1000 °C.
The modification should not introduce phase instability or degrade high‐temperature performance.
frame.regime: Mechanical performance is evaluated at room temperature and under high-temperature conditions up to approximately 1000 °C during load-bearing (strength) tests.
prior_attempts: The existing as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy has been optimized for strength at high temperatures, but its high density has remained a drawback.

Literature on related high-entropy alloys suggests that substitutions—such as replacing one of the heavier elements with a lighter one—can balance density reduction while maintaining strength. For example, previous studies on similar systems (e.g., HfNbMoTiZr) have shown that replacing a heavy element with a lighter but similarly refractory element can be beneficial.
frame.proposed_intervention_and_mechanism: Replace the heavy element tantalum (Ta) with niobium (Nb). Since Ta is one of the primary contributors to the high density (Ta has a density of ~16.65 g/cm³) and Nb has a significantly lower density (~8.57 g/cm³) while offering comparable high-temperature stability and strength, this substitution reduces the overall density. The mechanism is based on reducing the weighted average density of the alloy via atomic substitution that does not alter the high entropy nature or the significant lattice distortion that contributes to its excellent mechanical properties.
frame.predicted_directional_changes: Lower overall density from 10.21 g/cm³ toward a value closer to 8.6–9.0 g/cm³, while maintaining, or possibly even enhancing, the solid solution strengthening and high-temperature stability due to similar refractory characteristics between Nb and Ta.
frame.applicable_temperature_and_loading_bound: The revised alloy should perform similarly to the as-cast alloy at room temperature and under high-temperature conditions up to approximately 1000 °C, under mechanical loading conditions used for high-temperature strength tests (e.g., compression/tensile testing at elevated temperatures).
frame.supporting_prior_evidence: Prior work on high entropy alloys has demonstrated that substituting heavy elements with lighter ones (e.g., replacing Ta with Nb in related alloy systems) can yield lower density alloys without compromising high-temperature mechanical properties. Studies on systems such as HfNbMoTiZr support the notion that Nb can serve as an effective replacement for Ta with respect to high melting temperature and strength retention.
frame.proposed_experiment: Fabricate an alloy with the revised composition HfMoNbTiZr (replacing Ta entirely with Nb) using a similar as-cast processing route. Characterize the alloy’s density, microstructure (to ensure solid solution formation and a single-phase microstructure), and mechanical properties (strength and ductility) at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to ~1000 °C under controlled loading conditions. Compare these properties directly against the original HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
frame.rejection_criterion: If the Nb-substituted alloy exhibits a significant drop in mechanical strength or high-temperature stability (e.g., a reduction of strength by more than 10-15% or phase instability occurring near 1000 °C) compared to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, then the hypothesis that the single intervention (Ta→Nb substitution) can lower density without sacrificing mechanical performance would be falsified.

decision.trend: Earlier work in the field has typically focused on achieving excellent mechanical strength in high-entropy alloys via processing and compositional design while grappling with high density issues. In several studies, researchers have shown that substituting a heavy element with a lighter but similarly refractory element can reduce alloy density without a catastrophic loss in mechanical performance. For example, alloys containing both Ta and Nb (e.g., in equiatomic Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti systems) demonstrated that the presence of Nb contributes to lower overall density while retaining high-temperature stability. However, these studies were done with mixed contributions of both Ta and Nb rather than a complete replacement, and thus the behavior of a full substitution remains to be verified.
decision.unsolved: While partial replacement strategies have illustrated that incorporating Nb can reduce density, there is still uncertainty whether a single intervention—completely replacing Ta with Nb in HfMoTaTiZr—will maintain the solid solution strengthening and phase stability required for high mechanical performance at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (~1000 °C).
decision.lever: Replace Ta with Nb (full substitution to form HfMoNbTiZr)
decision.why: This intervention directly targets the density issue by removing a very heavy component (Ta) with a lighter element (Nb) known from related systems to retain refractory and strengthening characteristics. The trend in related high-entropy alloy research indicates that using Nb in place of Ta can lower the overall density while preserving, or even enhancing, solid solution strengthening, making it the most plausible next step to test the hypothesis within the same design frame.
